# Step 2.234, the independent review by attack (2026-11-27)

Reviewed at 562c262c on `lane/2.234-wrong-tries`, both adapters, the server code and the screens. Throwaway attacks (a vitest file beside the adapters, a browser script with scripts on) were run and deleted; nothing but this file is committed.

## Findings

**Medium 1. Minted device ids take a known device's code asks out of the network's cap, and multiply them for one address.** `packages/providers/src/sign-in/limit-subjects.ts:41` gives a vouched device the network key `known-device <id>`, so its asks never meet the network's 200 an hour, and the address's 5 an hour is per device id. The device id is whatever the browser's `srl_device` holds if it fits the shape (`apps/web/src/server/sign-in/device.ts:27`), and every successful sign-in adds a tag for it (`flows.ts:339`), so an account holder can make as many known devices for their own address as they like. How to see it: with the network's 200 used up and a stranger's ask refused, 20 device ids asked 6 reset codes each for one address: 100 codes were sent in one hour, on the local stand-in and on the Supabase adapter alike. Real harm: each ask is a `generate_link` call to Supabase and a mail from our sender (and each new-device sign-in another mail, T-70), so the mail bill and the sender's reputation have no per-network ceiling, only the bot check per sign-in and per ask. Narrowest fix: keep the plain network as the network key for a known device's code asks (only the address key is its own); optionally count all known devices of one address together.

**Medium 2. A stranger kills the owner's waiting code, known device or not.** One pending code per address (`packages/providers/src/sign-in/local/local-sign-in.ts:232`, `supabase/supabase-sign-in.ts:292`, and GoTrue keeps one), and its 5 tries are spent by anyone holding a flow for the address. How to see it: the owner's known device asks a reset code; a stranger on another network asks one (allowed, the address's stranger count), then types 5 wrong codes; the owner's own code and the newest code both answer `too-many-attempts`, on both adapters. Real harm: on a new device the owner's password is paused and "Reset your password" is the way in the screen names (S-133); a stranger cannot see when the owner asks, so with 5 asks an hour this kills a code only when it lands in the owner's minute or two, not a sure lock-out, but T-504's "its codes are counted on their own" is not true of the code itself. Narrowest fix: while a code asked by a known device is unexpired, an unknown device's ask for that address does not replace it (same answer to the asker, a mail with no code as for a reset without an account, so T-68 holds), and on the Supabase adapter no `generate_link` is made for it.

**Medium 3. Erasing an account leaves the address in the database under a known device's keys.** `erase_account` (`supabase/migrations/0012_accounts_and_sign_in_store.sql:517-519`) deletes `code_requests`, `guesses` and `guess_locks` rows only where the subject is exactly the address; the subjects `known-device <id> <address>` hold the address in plain text and are deleted only when the same subject is counted again (`packages/database/src/sign-in/count-code-request.ts:28-33`, `guess-counts.ts:59-64`), so for a device that never comes back they stay for good. The note's "a known device's expire within the hour" holds for the counts, not for the rows. Narrowest fix: a migration in which `erase_account` also deletes subjects ending in `' ' || lower(address)` that start `known-device `; or the subject carries a hash of the address instead of the address.

**Low 4. Password-again, a new password and a new address still share the address's and the network's count with strangers.** `local-sign-in.ts:507` (`reserveGuess(account.email, network)`, the same in `changePassword` and `startEmailChange`), `supabase-sign-in.ts:623`. Real harm: a stranger's ten wrong passwords for a signed-in coach's address, or a network's 100, pause that coach's sensitive actions for 15 minutes; ordinary signed-in use is untouched. Narrowest fix: these come with a live session, so count them on a key of the session's account (`account <id>`), apart from strangers.

**Low 5. A tag is tied to the address and never expires.** `known-device.ts:37`, kept for the device cookie's whole life. A shared tablet that once signed in keeps, after a password change or "sign out everywhere", its own 10 wrong passwords per lock for that address, not counted on the network, so whoever holds it has a guessing allowance apart from strangers'; after an address moves to another account the old devices keep theirs. Narrowest fix: put the day of the sign-in in the tag and refuse tags older than, say, 90 days.

**Low 6. A test gap.** With the address dropped from the tag by hand (`known-device.ts:37`, the "sign in to your own account, then attack another address on the same browser" hole), `known-device.test.ts` failed 2 of 5, but `flows.test.ts` passed all its cases: no flows case signs in to one address and then tries another on the same browser. Restored; `git diff` empty.

**Low 7. 200 codes an hour per network (T-507) on the real adapter.** Each sign-up ask is a `generate_link` of type `magiclink` (`supabase-sign-in.ts:261`), which makes a Supabase user, so one network can leave up to 200 unfinished Supabase users an hour (was 30), and send one mail each to 200 other people's addresses an hour, behind the bot check. One address is still 5 an hour from strangers: no flood of one mailbox except through Medium 1. The supervised session should check Supabase's limits and the cost of unfinished users when it raises them.

## Nothing found

- **Forging or moving `srl_known`.** The tag is HMAC-SHA-256 under an HKDF key of `SESSION_SECRET` or `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY`; `SESSION_SECRET` is trimmed and must be 32 characters (`apps/web/src/server/config-schema.ts:22,173`), so it cannot be empty; the made-up key per process is used only with neither set (the local stand-in). Many tags: only 43-character tags are compared, in constant time. A moved cookie is good only with its own `srl_device` (both http-only): that is cookie theft. Signed in to one's own account, another address is not vouched for (the tag binds the address; the unit test proves it).
- **T-68, in a browser with scripts on** (local stand-in, a fresh build): eleven wrong passwords each for an address with an account and one without, interleaved: the same problem on every try, the same words, status 200, the same cookies set (`srl_device`, `srl_typed`), `srl_known` never set, 150 to 212 ms against 156 to 188 ms. Seven reset asks each: the same, except that the address with an account was paused one ask earlier, because its owner's own sign-up ask was in the hour; an unfinished sign-up counts the same way, so it tells nothing about an account.
- **Checks that pass on a timeout.** None found in `known-device-test` (its code reader throws after 10 tries; at most 3 pauses tolerated) or `known-device-limits.test.ts` (made-up clock).

## T-504 by name

Sound where it matters: a stranger's count cannot shut out a known device, and the vouch cannot be forged. It over-claims in two places: "its codes are counted on their own" (the code is shared and killable, Medium 2) and "its own tries meet the same numbers" (the numbers are per device id, and ids are free to make for one's own address, Medium 1). Recommended: amend T-504 so a known device is apart from strangers on the address's count only, keeps the network's count for code asks, and its tag expires (Low 5).
